questions.question: What does encryption fundamentally do to data?
options: Compresses data to save storage space
Automatically detects malware inside a file
Permanently deletes the original data after backup
Converts plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using an algorithm and a key
questions.explanation: Plaintext ko ciphertext mein convert karna using an algorithm aur key — bina key ke garbage, key ke saath original data.

questions.question: What is the main difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
options: Symmetric is always slower than asymmetric
Symmetric encryption can only be used for video files
Asymmetric encryption doesn't require any key at all
Symmetric uses the same key for encryption and decryption; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair
questions.explanation: Symmetric: AES — same key encrypt aur decrypt karne ke liye, fast. Asymmetric: RSA — public key se encrypt, private key se decrypt, slower but more secure.

questions.question: Which analogy does the guide use to describe encryption?
options: A smoke detector sounding an alarm
Writing a diary in a secret code language only you understand
A guard checking IDs at a door
questions.explanation: Tumhara diary mein secret language likhna jaisa — sirf tumhe pata hai key kya hai, key ke saath padho, nahi to gibberish.

questions.question: Which encryption type is generally faster to perform?
options: Both are exactly equal in speed always
Neither type has a speed difference
questions.explanation: Symmetric (AES) fast hai kyunki same key use hoti hai; asymmetric (RSA) slower hai but more secure key exchange ke liye.

questions.question: Two people who have never met before need to securely exchange a secret key over the internet before they can start using fast symmetric encryption. Which type of encryption is typically used to solve this initial exchange problem?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric encryption (public/private key pair) securely key exchange karne ke liye use hoti hai, jiske baad fast symmetric encryption use ho sakti hai — yeh TLS handshake ka bhi core idea hai.

questions.question: What does End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) guarantee?
options: The message is automatically translated to any language
Only the sender and receiver can read the message — not even the service provider
The message is stored permanently on the provider's server
The message is visible to the service provider but not to third parties
questions.explanation: Message sirf sender ke device pe encrypt hota hai aur sirf receiver ke device pe decrypt hota hai — server bhi nahi padh sakta, even WhatsApp apne messages nahi padh sakta.

questions.question: According to the guide, which messaging feature is a notable exception where E2EE is NOT applied by default?
options: Telegram's normal chats (only Secret Chats use E2EE)
questions.explanation: Telegram ke Secret Chats hi E2EE use karte hain — normal chats E2EE nahi hain! Yeh ek common misconception hai.

questions.question: A government requests a messaging company hand over the plaintext content of a user's messages, but the company says it technically cannot comply because it never had access to the decrypted content. What technology explains this?
questions.explanation: E2EE ki wajah se company khud bhi messages padh nahi sakti — decryption sirf receiver ke device pe hota hai.

questions.question: Which protocol does WhatsApp use to implement its End-to-End Encryption?
questions.explanation: WhatsApp Signal Protocol use karta hai E2EE implement karne ke liye — Signal app khud bhi isi protocol pe based hai.

questions.question: Is regular email typically protected by End-to-End Encryption?
options: Only Gmail is E2EE, all others are not
No, regular email is not E2EE by default
Yes, all email is always E2EE
questions.explanation: Regular email E2EE nahi hai by default — isliye email provider technically content padh sakta hai (jab tak koi extra tool use na ho).

questions.question: What is AES?
options: A type of firewall used to filter web traffic
A government-approved symmetric encryption algorithm used as an industry standard
An authentication protocol for logging into websites
questions.explanation: US government approved symmetric encryption algorithm. AES-128, AES-192, AES-256 (key size) — industry gold standard.

questions.question: How practically breakable is AES-256 with today's computing power, according to the guide?
options: Crackable within a day using a normal laptop
Unbreakable — even a supercomputer would need billions of years
Easily crackable within a few hours
questions.explanation: AES-256 is unbreakable with today's computers — even supercomputer billions of years lagenge is se crack karne mein.

questions.question: Which of these commonly uses AES encryption, according to the guide?
options: Wi-Fi (WPA2), HTTPS, and disk encryption like BitLocker
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi (WPA2), HTTPS, file encryption, banking, WhatsApp messages, disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault) — tum daily AES use karte ho without knowing.

questions.question: Your laptop's disk encryption tool (BitLocker/FileVault) is protecting your files at rest. What underlying encryption algorithm is most likely doing the actual work?
questions.explanation: Disk encryption tools (BitLocker, FileVault) internally AES use karte hain — yeh symmetric encryption ka industry standard hai.

questions.question: AES stands for what?
questions.explanation: AES = Advanced Encryption Standard — industry gold standard symmetric encryption algorithm.

questions.question: What problem does PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) solve?
options: It blocks malware from running on a device
It verifies online identity, e.g., confirming that a website is genuinely who it claims to be
It compresses large files for faster transfer
questions.explanation: PKI public key pairs, digital certificates, Certificate Authorities (CA) ka poora framework hai — identity verify karta hai online.

questions.question: What role does a Certificate Authority (CA) play in PKI?
options: It stores all users' passwords in plaintext
It is a trusted issuer of digital certificates, like DigiCert or Let's Encrypt
questions.explanation: CA (Certificate Authority): trusted issuer (DigiCert, Let's Encrypt), Digital Certificate: identity proof, CRL: revoked certificates ki list.

questions.question: What does a CRL (Certificate Revocation List) contain?
options: A list of certificates that have been revoked and should no longer be trusted
A list of authorized VPN users
A list of all encrypted files on a server
A list of blocked IP addresses
questions.explanation: CRL: revoked certificates ki list — jo certificates ab valid nahi hain, unko track karne ke liye.

questions.question: Your browser shows a padlock and confirms a site is genuinely 'google.com' rather than a fake lookalike site. Which underlying framework makes this identity verification possible?
questions.explanation: PKI ka poora purpose hi identity verify karna hai online — CA-issued digital certificates ke through browser confirm karta hai ki site genuine hai.

questions.question: Which of these is a component of PKI, according to the guide?
questions.explanation: PKI ke components: CA, Digital Certificate, aur CRL — yeh sab milke online trust management system banate hain.

questions.question: What is a digital certificate?
options: A type of malware detection signature
A physical ID card issued by the government
An electronic document that proves an entity's identity and contains its public key
A backup copy of encrypted files
questions.explanation: Electronic document jo ek entity ki identity prove karta hai aur unki public key contain karta hai — CA issue karta hai.

questions.question: Which analogy does the guide use for a digital certificate?
options: A guard checking IDs at a building
A passport — issued by a trusted authority, with your details and an expiry date
questions.explanation: Passport jaisa — government (CA) ne issue kiya, tumhara photo aur details hain (public key), expiry date hai, tamper-proof features hain.

questions.question: What does the browser's padlock icon in the address bar represent?
options: That the website has no malware whatsoever
A valid digital certificate being presented by the website
That the website loads faster than others
questions.explanation: Browser ka padlock icon yahi hai — digital certificate present ho raha hai, matlab site apni identity prove kar rahi hai.

questions.question: Which of these is contained within a digital certificate, according to the guide?
options: The owner's public key and the issuing CA's digital signature
questions.explanation: Contains: owner name, public key, issuing CA, validity dates, domain name, CA's digital signature (tamper proof).

questions.question: A bank trusts a customer's document because it carries an official passport-like proof of identity issued by a recognized authority. What is the digital equivalent of this trust mechanism online?
options: A digital certificate issued by a Certificate Authority
questions.explanation: Bank ne passport dekha → trust kiya — online iska equivalent digital certificate hai jo CA ne issue kiya.

questions.question: What does a digital signature provide?
options: Automatic encryption of the entire hard drive
Proof that a document was signed by a specific person and hasn't been tampered with (non-repudiation)
A backup copy of the signed document
questions.explanation: Apni private key se document ko 'sign' karna — koi bhi tumhari public key se verify kar sakta hai ki document tumne hi sign kiya aur modify nahi hua. Non-repudiation provide karta hai.

questions.question: What is the first step in the digital signature process, according to the guide?
options: Send the document over an unencrypted channel
Compress the document into a zip file
Generate a hash of the document
questions.explanation: Process: 1. Document ka hash generate karo, 2. private key se hash encrypt karo (= signature), 3. Receiver same hash generate kar verify karta hai.

questions.question: Which key is used to create a digital signature, and which key is used to verify it?
options: No key is needed for either step
The signer's private key creates it; the signer's public key verifies it
The signer's public key creates it; the signer's private key verifies it
Both creation and verification use the same shared secret password
questions.explanation: Private key se hash encrypt karke signature banta hai; receiver public key se signature decrypt karke verify karta hai.

questions.question: A contract's recipient can mathematically prove the sender actually signed it and that no one altered even a single word afterward. Which security concept guarantees this?
questions.explanation: Digital signature non-repudiation provide karta hai — sender deny nahi kar sakta ki usne sign kiya, aur tampering bhi detect ho jaati hai.

questions.question: What security property specifically means 'the signer cannot later deny having signed the document'?
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation exactly yehi property hai — digital signature ka primary benefit.

questions.question: What is the current status of SSL, according to the guide?
options: Still the most current and secure protocol in use
Technically deprecated and replaced by TLS, though the term 'SSL' is still commonly used
Never existed — it was always called TLS
A hardware device used to encrypt disks
questions.explanation: Ab technically deprecated hai — TLS use hota hai, par 'SSL' term abhi bhi common usage mein hai.

questions.question: Why was SSL 3.0 specifically abandoned, according to the guide?
options: It required a paid license to use
It was too slow for modern internet speeds
It was never adopted by any browser
questions.explanation: SSL 3.0 mein POODLE vulnerability thi isliye abandon kiya gaya — TLS 1.0 se aage evolution hua.

questions.question: What is the correct chronological evolution from SSL to the current standard, according to the guide?
questions.explanation: SSL 2.0 (1995) → SSL 3.0 → TLS 1.0 → TLS 1.1 → TLS 1.2 → TLS 1.3 (current) — yeh sahi chronological order hai.

questions.question: A colleague refers to a website's 'SSL certificate,' even though the site is actually using the modern TLS protocol underneath. What does this illustrate?
options: SSL and TLS are entirely unrelated technologies
The colleague is completely wrong and the site is insecure
TLS is actually older than SSL
The term 'SSL' is still used colloquially even though TLS has replaced it technically
questions.explanation: Guide khud bolti hai 'SSL' term abhi bhi common hai, chahe technically TLS use ho raha ho — industry jargon mein legacy naming persist karta hai.

questions.question: What does SSL stand for?
questions.explanation: SSL = Secure Sockets Layer — secure communication protocol jo ab TLS se replace ho chuka hai.

questions.question: What is actually running behind the scenes when you use HTTPS today?
questions.explanation: Jab tum HTTPS use karte ho, actually TLS run ho raha hai — current secure communication protocol jo encryption, authentication, integrity teeno provide karta hai.

questions.question: What is the first step of a TLS handshake, according to the guide?
options: The client says 'Hello, I support TLS 1.3'
The server immediately sends encrypted data
The client sends its password in plaintext
questions.explanation: 1. Client: 'Hello, I support TLS 1.3', 2. Server: 'OK, here's my certificate', 3. Key exchange, 4. Encrypted communication begins.

questions.question: Which three properties does TLS provide together, according to the guide?
questions.explanation: TLS encryption, authentication, integrity — teeno provide karta hai simultaneously, sirf data hide karna nahi.

questions.question: During a connection setup, the server sends its certificate to the client, and both sides then exchange keys before any actual data is sent. What process is this describing?
questions.explanation: Yeh exactly TLS handshake ka process hai — hello, certificate exchange, key exchange, phir encrypted communication begins.

questions.question: What does TLS stand for?
questions.explanation: TLS = Transport Layer Security — SSL ka successor, internet ki backbone security protocol.

questions.question: What is HTTPS made of, according to the guide?
questions.explanation: HTTP (web protocol) + TLS (encryption) = HTTPS. Browser ka padlock icon = HTTPS.

questions.question: What common misconception does the guide correct about HTTPS?
options: HTTPS makes a website completely immune to hacking
HTTPS does not mean the site itself is trustworthy — it only means the connection is encrypted
HTTPS automatically blocks all phishing attempts
HTTPS is only used by government websites
questions.explanation: HTTPS = secure site NAHI. Sirf matlab hai connection encrypted hai. Fake phishing sites bhi HTTPS use karti hain. Padlock ≠ trustworthy website.

questions.question: A phishing website has a valid padlock icon and uses HTTPS, yet it is still designed to steal your login credentials. What does this demonstrate?
options: HTTPS automatically verifies a site's honesty
The browser has a bug if this occurs
HTTPS certificates are never issued to malicious sites, so this can't happen
HTTPS only guarantees an encrypted connection, not that the site itself is legitimate
questions.explanation: Exactly the misconception the guide warns about — fake phishing sites bhi HTTPS use kar sakti hain, padlock trustworthiness ki guarantee nahi deta.

questions.question: What does the padlock icon in a browser's address bar specifically indicate?
options: That the website has been manually reviewed by the browser vendor
That the website has no ads
That the website is hosted in the user's own country
That HTTPS (encrypted transit) is being used
questions.explanation: Padlock icon = HTTPS active hai, data encrypted hai transit mein — MITM attacker garbled text hi dekhega — but yeh site ki legitimacy guarantee nahi karta.

questions.question: If a MITM attacker intercepts traffic on an HTTPS-protected connection, what will they typically see?
options: The exact plaintext of the conversation
Only the sender's IP address in plaintext, nothing else
Garbled, encrypted text they cannot easily read
A full copy of the user's password in plaintext, always
questions.explanation: Data encrypted hai transit mein — MITM attacker garbled text hi dekhega, yehi HTTPS ka core protection hai.

questions.question: What is SSH primarily used for?
options: Securely accessing a remote server from the command line
questions.explanation: Remote server ko securely access karna command line se — web developers, system admins daily use karte hain.

questions.question: Which older, unencrypted protocol did SSH replace in 1995?
questions.explanation: Telnet (unencrypted predecessor) ko replace kiya 1995 mein — SSH ne encrypted alternative provide kiya.

questions.question: What is a more secure alternative to password login when using SSH?
options: SSH keys, where the public key sits on the server and the private key stays with the user
Sharing the same password across all servers
questions.explanation: Password ke alawa SSH keys use kar sakte ho — more secure. Public key server pe, private key tumhare paas — brute force practically impossible.

questions.question: A system administrator connects to a remote Linux server to run commands, and the entire session is encrypted so no one on the network can see the commands or their output. Which protocol enables this?
questions.explanation: SSH exactly is use case ke liye design hui hai — encrypted remote server access via command line.

questions.question: Why is brute-forcing an SSH connection secured with SSH keys considered 'practically impossible'?
options: Because SSH blocks all connection attempts automatically
Because SSH doesn't allow remote connections at all
Because the private key never leaves the user's device and isn't a guessable password
Because SSH keys expire every second
questions.explanation: Private key kabhi network pe transmit nahi hoti aur itni complex hoti hai ki brute force practically impossible ho jaata hai.
